extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) and applicants drafting improvement claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting Jepson (improvement) claims that identify conventional preamble elements and recite the point(s) of novelty as the improvement. Covers required claim structure, relevant regulatory template, risks from implied prior-art admissions, and appropriate use-cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Jepson claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A Jepson claim is a method or product claim where one or more limitations are specifically identified as a point of novelty, distinguishable over at least the contents of the preamble. The preamble makes a statement about the state of the prior art, and then claims an improvement over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this format when the claim explicitly separates known/conventional subject matter (preamble) from the claimed improvement. The definition emphasizes that the claimed improvement is presented as distinct from what is stated in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson claim structure and format
rubrics_metrics.description: A Jepson claim has a specific format: 1) A preamble that identifies conventional/known features of the claimed subject matter; 2) A specific transitional phrase (e.g., "wherein the improvement comprises"); 3) A recitation of the "new or improved" aspects of the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the three-part layout in the claim text. Example wording: "A system for storing information having (...) wherein the improvement comprises:" The transitional phrase should clearly signal which limitations are conventional and which are the improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory template (37 C.F.R. 1.75(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvement patent claims should follow a specific template with three components: 1) A preamble comprising a general description of all the elements or steps of the claimed combination which are conventional or known; 2) A phrase such as "wherein the improvement comprises"; 3) Those elements, steps, and/or relationships which constitute that portion of the claimed combination which the applicant considers as the new or improved portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and conform to 37 C.F.R. 1.75(e) when drafting Jepson-format claims to ensure the claim language matches the regulatory expectation for improvement claims. Use the regulatory phrasing to clearly delineate the known versus new portions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-art admission risk when using Jepson format
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafting a claim in Jepson format is taken as an implied admission that the subject matter of the preamble is the prior art work of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implied admission can facilitate examiners' or accused infringers' arguments that the improvement is obvious in light of the admitted prior art under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a). Because of this risk, Jepson claim style is seldom used in modern U.S. practice. Consider alternate claim drafting strategies unless the admission is harmless or beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate circumstances to use Jepson claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Jepson claims may be appropriate when the patentee is attempting to overcome, or prevent, a double patenting rejection, particularly when avoiding double patenting over the patentee's own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used to avoid double patenting over the patentee's own earlier work, the Jepson format generally causes no deleterious effects. An examiner may also suggest Jepson format to clearly delineate that the patent will only cover the improvement and not the underlying work. Use Jepson only when its benefits (e.g., resolving double patenting issues or complying with an examiner's direction) outweigh the risk of admitting conventional subject matter as prior art.
